picked.t: Vietnam motorbike tours offer different way to explore country
picked.body: Motorbike travel offers visitors a way to explore Vietnam beyond major tourist destinations, from winding northern mountain roads to forested central routes and riverside villages in the Mekong Delta. Unlike conventional sightseeing tours, motorcycle journeys allow travelers to explore at their own pace, stopping at local markets, rural communities and lesser-known attractions. Organized tours also provide local guides, route planning and logistical support. Northern Vietnam is popular with adventure riders for its mountainous terrain, limestone formations and winding roads. North Vietnam motorbike tours often include routes through Ha Giang, Cao Bang and Sa Pa, passing through valleys, terraced fields and villages inhabited by ethnic minority communities such as the Hmong, Dao and Tay. One of the region's best-known routes crosses Ma Pi Leng Pass, which overlooks the Nho Que River and surrounding limestone cliffs. Its steep slopes and sharp bends require experience, particularly in rainy or low-visibility conditions. In central Vietnam, sections of the historic Ho Chi Minh Trail offer a mix of natural scenery and wartime heritage. Riders can travel along the Truong Son mountain range, visit historical sites around Khe Sanh and explore the caves and countryside of Phong Nha-Ke Bang National Park. Further south, the Mekong Delta offers a slower-paced experience, with relatively flat roads connecting orchards, coconut groves, canals and rural communities. Travelers can visit riverside towns, cross waterways by local ferry and explore traditional markets, although narrow roads and traffic still require caution. Beyond the scenery, Vietnam motorcycle tours provide opportunities to experience local life. Guided itineraries often include village visits, market stops and overnight stays at family-run accommodations. In northern mountain areas, some tours offer homestays in traditional stilt houses, where visitors can sample regional dishes such as freshwater fish, smoked meats, mountain vegetables and bamboo shoots. These shared meals and interactions with host families can offer insight into local customs and food traditions. Riders should avoid alcohol before and during their journeys. Motorcycle travel requires preparation, especially on mountain routes where weather, road surfaces and visibility can change quickly. Choosing a suitable bike is important. Lightweight dual-sport models such as the Honda CRF300L and CRF250L are designed for mixed terrain, while adventure motorcycles such as the CFMOTO 450MT may suit some routes. Riders should consider the motorcycle's weight, handling, seat height and luggage capacity, as well as their own experience. Protective equipment should include a certified helmet, riding jacket, gloves, abrasion-resistant trousers and sturdy boots. Foreign visitors should check Vietnam's licensing requirements before riding. Depending on their nationality and license category, an International Driving Permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention may be recognized when accompanied by the relevant national driving license. Travelers should confirm that their documents cover the motorcycle category they intend to ride and that their insurance includes motorcycle use in Vietnam. For remote mountain routes, an experienced local guide can help with navigation, accommodation and mechanical problems. Some guided tours also provide support vehicles, spare parts and assistance in areas with limited mobile coverage. Hanoi-based operator Vietnam Motorbike Tour Expert offers organized motorcycle journeys across the country. From northern mountain passes and central Vietnam's historic trails to the Mekong Delta's rural roads, motorbike tours offer an alternative way to explore the country's regional landscapes and communities. Proper equipment, valid documentation and careful route planning are essential for a safer journey.

picked.t: Vietnamese duo quit $57,000 jobs to sell street food in Canada
picked.body: At lunchtime, nearly every red and blue plastic chair at their Toronto eatery is occupied. Customers chat while enjoying snacks such as mixed rice paper salad ( banh trang tron ), sweet soup che , and rice paper rolls ( banh trang cuon ). Vietnamese-language signs adorn the walls, recreating the atmosphere of casual street-side eateries in Ho Chi Minh City. Behind the business are Kim Ngoc and My Loan, both 29, who opened their first Premium Banh outlet in October 2024 using savings accumulated over years of working. By August 2026, they had their third outlet and around 20 employees. The duo moved to Canada in 2017 to study culinary arts. After graduating and gaining work experience, they met while working at a steakhouse in Toronto. Both grew up in HCMC and shared a fondness for Vietnamese street food. Whenever they craved a familiar dish, they would ask friends and relatives coming from Vietnam to bring rice paper. Their search for familiar flavors made them realize there was demand for Vietnamese street food in Toronto. Giving up stable jobs and good salaries to sell Vietnamese snacks was not an easy decision. "We figured that since we're still young, we might as well give it a try," they explain. In October 2024, they invested their savings to open their first outlet. "We want Vietnamese customers to rediscover familiar flavors and offer foreigners a chance to explore popular Vietnamese street foods," Ngoc says. Around 70% of their ingredients, including dried beef and dried shrimp, are imported from Vietnam, while fresh meat, vegetables, and eggs are sourced locally. The pair pay attention to small details to preserve the original flavors. For banh trang tron , for instance, they use kumquat instead of regular lime to achieve its characteristic sourness. A serving of mixed rice paper salad costs CAD13-14 (US$9.12-9.82) while other snacks range from CAD10-20; desserts and drinks are priced at CAD7-11. Building business from scratch The first 18 months were challenging. Ngoc and Loan took responsibility for almost every aspect of the business, from finding locations and renovating premises to sourcing ingredients, recruiting employees, managing finances, developing recipes, and monitoring food quality. The business initially brought in too little money, meaning the two were without a regular income to take care of their living expenses for a longish period. They relied on their savings and reducing their spending from around CAD4,000 each to CAD1,500. They also had to navigate Canadian business regulations and food safety standards while establishing a reliable supply chain for their ingredients. Loan recalls the difficult days: "There were times when the work left us completely exhausted; some nights, we barely slept at all. We just kept encouraging each other, reminding ourselves that even a small improvement over the previous day was a win." A turning point came last year when they took their food to a Vietnamese culinary festival in Canada. Their stall attracted long queues from the moment it opened comprising both Vietnamese expatriates and locals. Following the event, many visitors sought out their restaurant and recommended it to friends and family, helping the business build a stable customer base. Ngoc remembers one customer who tried banh trang cuon for the first time and was surprised by the combination of flavors. "She took a bite and exclaimed, 'Wow!'—she hadn't expected it to be so delicious. In the west, people are familiar with mango smoothies, but the idea of using mango inside rice paper rolls was completely new to them. When she learned the dish originated in Vietnam, she said, 'Oh my goodness, why didn't I discover this sooner?' She ended up coming back every single week." As the brand expanded to multiple locations, maintaining consistent food quality became another challenge. Ngoc and Loan developed standardized ingredient measurements, seasoning ratios and preparation procedures for every dish, particularly banh trang tron and their varieties of che . Their focus has shifted from establishing the business to building a sustainable Vietnamese food brand in Canada. "Rapid expansion is certainly welcome, but the most important thing is to maintain quality and a genuine passion for the food," the two add.

picked.t: Nhaan Resort & Spa Hoi An introduces riverside seafood restaurant Plait
picked.body: Located along the Co Co River, Plait sources seafood from local suppliers, including Duy Hai Fish Market in Hoi An. Depending on the daily catch and season, selections may include golden rabbitfish, silver pomfret and moray eel. Diners can choose their seafood and preparation method, including charcoal grilling in a Josper oven or hot-pot cooking. Executive chef Duong Danh Linh, who grew up in central Vietnam, leads the restaurant's culinary program, which combines regional ingredients with traditional cooking methods. Plait also offers cooking classes through the resort's "Meet the Artisans" program, which introduces guests to local crafts and traditions through experiences with artisans from Thanh Ha Pottery Village and Kim Bong Carpentry Village. For the cooking classes, guests visit a local market with the chef in the morning to learn about seasonal produce and seafood brought in by fishing boats. Back at the resort, they take part in a "No Menu" session, preparing dishes based on the ingredients available that day before enjoying their meals at Plait. Signature dishes include Tan Thanh squid seared on volcanic stone and Ninh Hoa Babylon snails flambéed at the table. Yellowfin tuna from Phu Yen is dry-aged before grilling, while whole fish can be baked in clay and opened at the table. Other options include raw and chilled seafood, wok-fried dishes, Quang Nam tiger prawns, Binh Ba lobster and wagyu beef. The menu also features oyster congee and desserts inspired by local specialties, including Hoi An-style tau pho , a traditional tofu pudding. The beverage menu includes cocktails inspired by the town's landscape and culture, such as Lantern Glow, referencing its lantern-lit streets, and Garden Breeze, inspired by its gardens and natural surroundings. Sridhar Thota, general manager of Nhaan Resort & Spa Hoi An, said Plait aims to introduce visitors to Central Vietnamese cuisine through locally sourced ingredients and interactive dining. "At Nhaan Resort & Spa Hoi An, we empower travelers to explore the rich cultural traditions of central Vietnam. Plait brings the restaurant's vision to life with an interactive approach to gastronomy, where our chefs showcase Central Vietnamese cuisine and elevate it with contemporary techniques," he said. Plait is one of four dining venues at the resort, alongside Keng, an all-day dining restaurant; Bong Lounge, a riverside bar; and Nipa Pool Bar, which offers poolside dining. Located in Vong Nhi Village, about five kilometers from Hoi An Ancient Town and 750 meters from Cua Dai Beach, the resort has 174 rooms and suites. Designed by Vietnamese architect Vo Trong Nghia, the property draws on the area's traditional architecture and the craftsmanship of Kim Bong Carpentry Village. Its facilities include an outdoor swimming pool, an eforea spa and health club, meeting and event spaces, and activities introducing guests to local traditions. Nhaan Resort & Spa Hoi An is part of Tapestry Collection by Hilton, a portfolio of hotels and resorts with individual identities shaped by their destinations. For more information about Plait or reservations, visit the resort's official website or email dadha_reservations@hilton.com.

picked.t: Afghan visa overstayer in Vietnam faces prosecution for smuggling 56 compatriots into Cambodia
picked.body: The Ho Chi Minh City People's Procuracy recently issued an indictment prosecuting Mohammadi Mukhtar, 31, Du Duy Trung, 41, from Tay Ninh Province, and Le Dinh Chinh, 41, for organizing others' illegal exit from the country. The indictment says Mukhtar entered Vietnam from Cambodia through the Moc Bai International Border Gate in Tay Ninh on April 21, 2024, on a tourist visa valid until July 10 that year. He stayed on after it expired. During that time, he colluded with Trung and Chinh to send Afghans into Cambodia illegally through unofficial border crossings. Fee at every step In December 2024, Mukhtar agreed with a person named Ramozi Ahmad Hussain, whose background is unknown, to bring Afghans into Vietnam on tourist visas and then move them to Cambodia for VND7.5 million ($289) per person. For those without Vietnamese visas, Mukhtar passed their passport details and portrait photos to an unidentified woman who handled their tourist visa applications, at $150 per person. To get them across the border, Mukhtar struck a deal with Trung at VND4.5 million ($174) per person. Trung then hired someone named Hung, whose identity is also unknown, to take them across for VND2.5 million ($96) each, and hired Chinh to drive them for VND900,000 ($35) per person. Once the Afghans arrived in Vietnam, Mukhtar put them up in hotels and told Trung where they were. Trung then had Chinh pick them up by car and take them to the crossing area. From February to March 2025, the three organized illegal exits to Cambodia for 20 Afghans on four occasions. Between December 2024 and April 2025, they sent another 36 Afghans across through unofficial routes, but investigators could not establish who they were. Bank statements show Mukhtar received more than VND487 million ($18,800) in fees from the Afghans. On June 13, 2025, the security investigation agency of the Ho Chi Minh City Police ordered the arrest and detention of Mukhtar, Trung and Chinh for investigation.

picked.t: South Korea's top university considers $748 monthly stipend, free tuition for first foreign-only class
picked.body: "Because we expect to select only a small number of students initially, we are preparing to provide scholarships to all of them," Noh Yoo-sun, the SNU College dean overseeing the launch of the Global Talent Division, told The Korea Herald . Under the plan, students would receive the support for roughly their first three semesters, a period Noh described as "incubation" before they enter their majors. The division will admit international students without requiring them to declare a major. Students are expected to spend about two to three semesters on intensive Korean-language and foundational courses before moving into eligible majors across 10 colleges. "The amount has not been finalized yet," Noh said. "What we are currently considering is full tuition and 1 million won a month in living expenses." SNU expects a first cohort of about 36 students but will set no fixed quota, he said, with the final number depending on the size of the applicant pool and how many candidates the university considers sufficiently qualified. Noh said student support, including scholarships, can play a decisive role in the competition for top students, citing Vietnamese students admitted to SNU who chose the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) instead. About nine students have made a similar choice, he said. "If we want to attract outstanding students, what the university can offer those students becomes very important," he said. He acknowledged that offering the division's students better scholarships than other international students admitted through SNU's special admissions for foreigners could raise fairness concerns. SNU is also considering charging students in the division higher tuition than Korean students, partly because they will receive extra support such as intensive Korean-language classes and one-on-one peer tutoring, Noh said. The amount has not been set and would need approval through the university's tuition-setting process. If the scholarship package is finalized, however, the first cohort would have its tuition fully covered during the premajor period. Noh said SNU is still building the systems needed to recruit, teach and support more international undergraduates, including stronger Korean-language instruction, tailored foundational courses and better access to housing and other student services. The university expects the division to expand as those systems become established, he said. The scholarship model is likely to change as the division grows. Noh said SNU may eventually offer different levels of support or limit scholarships to selected students rather than the whole cohort. SNU is targeting Vietnam as one of five priority recruitment markets for the division, alongside mainland China, Taiwan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, Korea JoongAng Daily reported in October. SNU College faculty and staff are scheduled to visit Vietnam in January 2027 to present admissions guidelines, the newspaper said. Applicants and both their parents must be foreign nationals, according to SNU's admissions office. The scholarship plan is part of SNU's push to attract stronger international applicants and raise its relatively small number of international undergraduates. The university placed 38th in the 2027 QS World University Rankings, the highest of any South Korean university. Vietnamese students became the largest group of international students in South Korean higher education this year, making up 31.5% of 307,464 and overtaking Chinese students for the first time, according to Education Ministry data released in August.

picked.t: Vietnam's largest island Phu Quoc reports $2.4B tourism revenues in 10 months
picked.body: The Vietnam's largest island received 9.2 million tourist arrivals in the first 10 months, up 30% year-on-year, including 2.14 million foreign tourists, a 59% increase year-on-year and surpassing its full-year goal of 2 million. In October alone, the island generated VND5.1 trillion in tourism revenues, up 37.8% year-on-year as foreign tourist arrivals surged 50% to 223,000, according to An Giang Province's Department of Tourism. The strong growth reflects Phu Quoc's growing appeal as a holiday destination, underpinned by investment in tourism infrastructure and a wider range of visitor experiences. Improved air connectivity has also helped attract international visitors, with direct flights linking the island to key markets such as South Korea, Central Asia and Eastern Europe. Phu Quoc's peak tourist season runs from November to April, coinciding with the island's dry season, which typically brings sunny weather, calm seas and low humidity.

picked.t: Vietnam's top leader to attend APEC summit in China
picked.body: The trip, running from Nov. 17 to 20, is at the invitation of Chinese Communist Party General Secretary and President Xi Jinping. The Vietnamese leader will be accompanied by his wife, Ngo Phuong Ly, according to a statement from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Since its founding in 1989, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum has established itself as the region's premier economic cooperation mechanism. It continues to spearhead efforts promoting economic, trade, and investment liberalization on both regional and global scales. These initiatives have contributed to economic growth, peace, stability, and development across the Asia-Pacific. APEC focuses on three primary pillars: trade and investment liberalization, business facilitation, and economic and technical cooperation. This final pillar emphasizes capacity building alongside equitable, sustainable development. The forum's 21 member economies represent approximately 37% of the global population, 62% of world GDP, and 48% of global trade. Vietnam joined the bloc in 1998. APEC members are vital to Vietnam's economy, bringing together 15 of the nation's 30 strategic and comprehensive partners. These economies account for more than 77% of Vietnam's overall trade, nearly 81% of its foreign direct investment, and over 85% of its tourism. Of the 19 free trade agreements (FTAs) Vietnam has either implemented or is currently negotiating, 13 involve APEC members. Seventeen of the forum's 21 members are Vietnam's FTA partners. China, the summit's host nation, holds deep historical ties with Vietnam. China became the first country to establish diplomatic relations with Vietnam, on Jan. 18, 1950. The two nations formed a comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership in 2008. In 2023, they issued a joint statement elevating this partnership to build a "Vietnam-China community with a shared future" carrying strategic significance. During To Lam's state visit to China in April, both sides released another joint statement pledging to further deepen this partnership in the new era. Economic ties between the two nations remain robust. In 2025, China stood as Vietnam's largest trading partner while Vietnam was China's top trading partner within ASEAN and its fourth-largest globally. Chinese investment in Vietnam is also substantial. As of late October 2026, China had over 7,487 active projects in Vietnam with total registered capital exceeding $38.15 billion. This places China sixth out of 154 countries and territories investing in the nation. Tourism figures further highlight this close relationship. Vietnam welcomed 5.28 million Chinese visitors in 2025, a 41.3% year-on-year increase. These visitors accounted for a quarter of all international arrivals, making China the largest source market for foreign tourists in Vietnam.

picked.t: Atlas Air could double Vietnam operations if infrastructure improves: CEO
picked.body: "We could probably double the size of our operation here over the next several years," Steen told VnExpress International. The U.S.-based company has recorded 1,269 flight movements in Vietnam so far this year, up over 3,200% from 2016. It runs about 12 weekly frequencies to Hanoi. Steen said that level of activity is probably close to the maximum the existing infrastructure can handle, even though demand could support further growth. Atlas needs more parking stands that can accommodate large freighters such as the Boeing 747-8, along with warehouses and ground handling capacity to prepare pallets and containers for export. Digital platforms for exchanging transport documents and other shipment information are also essential, he said. While new facilities are being built, Vietnam could make better use of existing capacity by improving coordination, communication and operational planning. "You can always optimize utilization of existing infrastructures," Steen said. On the demand side, expanding manufacturing creates more business for operators connecting Vietnam’s factories with overseas markets. Atlas bases its deployment decisions on where manufacturers and customers need capacity. "Manufacturing is always going to attract logistics providers," Steen said. AI investment and data-center construction are adding to that demand, creating time-sensitive shipments of semiconductors and other high-value electronic components. "Components for data centers are being manufactured in Vietnam and other Southeast Asian destinations and then flown into the U.S. for final assembly," he said. Most freight on Atlas’ Vietnam operations consists of high-tech products, Steen said, naming HP and Dell among the manufacturers. Through July, Atlas carried 39% of cargo flown nonstop from Vietnam to the U.S. by American carriers. Vietnam’s broader air cargo market is also expanding. Cargo throughput at Vietnamese airports reached approximately 1.6 million tonnes in the first 10 months, up 9.6% from the same period last year, according to the Civil Aviation Authority of Vietnam (CAAV). Although air cargo represents a small share of total freight volume, it accounts, on average, for about 30% of the value of Vietnam’s imports and exports across all transport modes, the authority said. To accommodate growing demand, Vietnam is investing in new airports that could help ease the capacity constraints Steen described. "Vietnam is doing a lot of the right things at the moment," he said. "Putting capital into infrastructure is absolutely critical, both on the passenger side as well as the cargo side." In the south, Long Thanh International Airport is expected to begin commercial operations on Dec. 24, 2026, according to plans reported by the Airports Corporation of Vietnam and the CAAV. Its first phase is designed to handle 1.2 million tonnes of cargo annually. In the north, Gia Binh International Airport is targeting commercial operations by the end of 2028 and is planned to handle 1.6 million tonnes of cargo a year by 2030. "It’s going to help us as operators operate more effectively and efficiently," Steen said of infrastructure investment. "It’s going to help us add more capacity."

picked.t: 현대車 , 베트남 신차 판매량 ‘뚝’…10월 3,400여 대 전월比 11.6%↓
picked.body: 하노이 짱띠엔플라자에 전시된 현대차 팰리세이드 하이브리드. (사진=현대자동차)  지난달 현대자동차의 베트남 신차 판매량이 두 자릿수 감소한 것으로 나타났다. 현대차 베트남 조립·판매업체 현대탄꽁(Hyundai Thanh Cong·TC모터)이 11일 내놓은 ‘2026년 10월 판매 실적’ 보고서에 따르면, 지난 10월 한 달간 베트남 시장 현대차 신차 인도 대수는 3,422대로 집계됐다. 전월과 비교하면 11.6% 감소한 것이다. 10월 기준 누적 판매 대수는 3만8,834대를 기록했다. 올 들어 월평균 베트남 내 신차 판매량이 3,883대에 이른 셈이다. 지난달 모델별 판매량은 크레타가 783대로 가장 많았다. 전월과 비교하면 66대 감소한 것이나, 누적 판매 대수는 7,632대로 현대차 라인업 가운데 1위를 지켰다. 다음으로는 투싼이 761대(누적 7,477대)로 2위를 달렸다. 대형 SUV인 팰리세이드는 10월 한 달간 219대가 판매됐다. 현대탄꽁은 10월 신형 팰리세이드 하이브리드 판매가를 발표하고, 전국적으로 차량 인도를 시작했다. 현대탄꽁은 팰리세이드 하이브리드 모델을 추가하며 대형 SUV 시장에서 입지 확대를 모색하고 있다. 그 외 승용차 모델로는 △i10 108대 △액센트 158대 △싼타페 96대 △스타게이저 153대 등의 판매고를 올렸다. 승용차와 더불어 상용차는 10월 1,038대, 누적으로는 1만1,725대가 판매되며 실적을 뒷받침했다. 이에 대해 현대탄꽁 관계자는 “상용차는 운송과 생산, 서비스업 등 전국 산업 현장에 공급되고 있으며, 판매 구조에서 차지하는 비중이 큰 편”이라고 설명했다. 현대탄꽁은 하반기 들어 프로모션과 금융 지원, 고객 관리 정책을 지속하고 있다. 회사는 연말까지 고객 혜택을 더 늘리고, 전국 유통망을 활용해 베트남에서 현대차 브랜드 입지를 강화한다는 계획이다.
